Can an 11-Year-Old Work Legally?

No, an 11-year-old cannot land a standard job as an employee, but they are fully allowed to earn money through casual work

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), children under 14 generally cannot be employed in most non-farm jobs.

That’s why an 11-year-old generally can’t get a regular job at McDonald’s, Burger King, Walmart, or another major employer.

Jobs

However, federal law includes specific exceptions and boundaries that make earning money at 11 completely legal:

  • Casual Self-Employment: When an 11-year-old walks a neighbor’s dog, rakes leaves, washes cars, or cuts grass, they are operating as a self-employed individual, not a hired employee.
  • Statutory Exemptions: Federal law explicitly allows kids under 14 to work as babysitters, deliver newspapers, or act in movies and theater.
  • Family-Owned Businesses: Kids of any age can work for a business owned entirely by their parents, provided the work isn’t in manufacturing, mining, or hazardous occupations.

Does an 11-year-old need a work permit?

Federal law doesn’t require work permits for the usual jobs that preteen kids do.

While states often require permits for 14- and 15-year-olds taking traditional jobs, these rules don’t apply to an 11-year-old doing casual neighborhood chores for cash.

Merchant Services & Payment Systems

Bottom line: An 11-year-old generally can’t be hired for a regular job, but there are legal ways for kids this age to earn money through permitted work and casual neighborhood services.

Neighborhood  jobs are usually the easiest place for an 11-year-old to start because a parent can help find customers, check out the work beforehand, and stay nearby if needed.

They also avoid the transportation problem that comes with jobs farther from home.

1. Dog Walking & Pet Sitting

Walking a neighbor’s dog is one of the easiest first jobs an 11 year old kid can try, and it’s a smaller version of the dog walking jobs adults get paid for.

Plenty of people love their dogs but don’t always want to make that 6 p.m. walk after a long day.

You could walk a neighbor’s dog, feed a cat while the owner is away, or stop by to check on someone’s pet.

The best part is that you can turn one  job into a regular one. If someone needs their dog walked every afternoon, that could give you steady weekly income.

Pet sitting can also bring in extra money when a neighbor goes out of town, although those pet sitting jobs are usually temporary.

Management

How much should an 11-year-old charge for dog walking?

Professional dog walkers often charge around $16 to $25 for a 30-minute walk.

You don’t need to match that rate at 11.

I’d start around $5 to $10 per walk for a simple neighborhood job.

For pet sitting, I’d charge by the visit rather than trying to copy professional pet-care rates.

A quick stop to feed a cat and refill its water is much different from spending several hours caring for multiple pets, so price the job based on the time and responsibility involved.

How to start

Start with a pet your family already knows. Before you take the job, have a parent meet the owner and go over the pet’s routine, including feeding, walking, and anything else you need to know.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

For the first few walks or visits, it’s a good idea for a parent to stay nearby.

I’d also start with easy-to-handle pets. If you can’t physically control a dog, don’t walk it.

2. Yard Cleanup: Raking, Weeding & Watering

Yard work is the classic kid job for a reason.

It’s simple, people always need it, and an 11-year-old can do most of it with tools the homeowner already owns.

Legal

Think raking leaves, bagging them, pulling weeds, and watering plants.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

Why it can work

You can also turn yard cleanup into repeat work, especially during fall leaf season. A homeowner might hire you again after a storm or whenever the yard needs another cleanup.

Keep in mind this is cleanup, not mowing. Lawn mowers and other power equipment can have age restrictions under federal and state child labor laws, so an 11-year-old should not simply be handed a mower and sent to work alone.

How much should an 11-year-old charge for yard work?

A professional lawn service usually starts at around $50 or more per visit. At least, that’s what I see here in St. Louis.

Jobs

So, if you’re 11, charging $10 to $25 for a yard cleanup is reasonable, depending on the size of the yard and how much work it needs.

A small job might take less than an hour. A large yard covered in heavy leaves could take much longer.

How to start

Start with neighbors your family already knows.

Before you give them a price, take a look at the yard so you can see how much work it actually needs. Then agree on exactly what you’ll do, whether that means raking leaves, pulling weeds, bagging yard waste, or watering plants.

If possible, bring your own rake, bags, and other basic hand tools.

Stick to hand tools and avoid power equipment, especially lawn mowers.

3. Washing Cars

A driveway car wash is a simple warm-weather job that doesn’t require much equipment.

Delivery Driver Jobs

Your child can wash a neighbor’s car with a hose, bucket, car soap, and sponge.

How much should an 11-year-old charge to wash a car?

Based on what I have seen on social media, kids offering simple car-washing services usually charge around $5 to $15 per vehicle.

Your price can go up if you include extras such as tire cleaning or an interior wipe-down.

Job Listings

Pro tip MP

Give people two options. You could charge less for an exterior wash and a little more for an exterior wash plus a quick interior wipe-down.

How to get your first customer

Start with family, friends, or neighbors you already know.

Have your child make a simple offer, such as:

“I can wash your car for $10 this Saturday.”

Giving someone a specific price and time makes it much easier to say yes than simply asking if they might want their car washed sometime.

After your child finishes the first few  jobs, ask each customer if they know a neighbor who might want a car wash, too.

Legal

Your child can also hand out or put a simple flyer on nearby doors with your help.

For the first few jobs, I’d keep everything close to home so your child doesn’t have to travel between customers.

4. Trash-Can Valet

This is one of the simplest recurring jobs your 11-year-old can offer.

Your child takes a neighbor’s trash and recycling bins to the curb before pickup, then brings them back afterward.

For some people, especially older or busy neighbors, this small chore is worth paying for every week.

How much should you charge?

Curb trash-can service can bring in $5 to $10 per house each month.

Jobs

Since the  job only takes a few minutes and gives you recurring customers, the small payments can add up.

For example, if your child gets 10 houses at $7 each, that’s $70 a month for the same basic chore.

How to get customers

I’d start with one street or a small group of nearby homes. That way, your child doesn’t waste time walking long distances between houses and can handle several customers on the same route.

Your child could simply say:

“I can take your trash and recycling bins out and bring them back every week for $7 a month.”

They can even offer the first week free so your neighbor can see how much easier it makes their week.

5. Weeding & Small Garden Help

A lot of homeowners need help keeping flower beds and small gardens under control, and your child can do much of this work with basic hand tools.

Your 11-year-old can pull weeds, water plants, spread mulch by hand, or help with simple planting.

How much should an 11-year-old charge for weeding?

$10 to $20 per session is a reasonable starting point, depending on the size of the area and how much work it needs. For a bigger job, agree on the price before your child starts.

This can also turn into repeat work because gardens need attention throughout the growing season.

6. Curb address painting

Curb address painting has become a popular kid and teen side hustle on YouTube and TikTok, where young people show before-and-after videos of repainting faded house numbers.

The idea is simple: your child offers to refresh faded or hard-to-read numbers on a home’s curb for a small fee.

How much can an 11-year-old make painting curb numbers?

You could charge $15 to $30 per address to start, depending on the size of the numbers and how much work is involved.

Job Listings

Three $20 addresses would put $60 in your child’s pocket from a few nearby customers.

What supplies are needed?

The startup cost can be fairly low.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

A basic kit can include:

  • Number stencils
  • Exterior paint suitable for the curb surface
  • Painter’s tape
  • A shield or covering to protect the surrounding area from paint

Your child can start small and use their first earnings to replace or upgrade supplies.

How to find curb painting customers

Start with neighbors, family friends, and other people you already know.

Look for homes where the curb numbers are faded, chipped, or difficult to read.

A simple pitch could be:

“Hi! I’m offering to refresh faded curb numbers in the neighborhood. I can repaint yours for $20.”

Before-and-after photos can also help your child show potential customers what the finished work looks like.

Is curb address painting safe for an 11-year-old?

This job needs close parent supervision because the work takes place near the street.

Jobs

An adult should stay with your child, help with setup, and make sure they stay safely away from traffic.

Before starting, check your local rules and any neighborhood or HOA restrictions on curb painting and door-to-door solicitation.

Summer Jobs for 11-Year-Olds

Summer break gives an 11-year-old something they don’t have during the school year: more free time during the day.

7. Running a Cold-Drink or Produce Stand

Think of this as a lemonade stand with a little more variety.

Your 11-year-old could sell cold drinks on a hot day or offer extra tomatoes, peppers, or other produce from your family garden.

How much can an 11-year-old make?

There’s no set amount. Your child’s profit is what’s left after you subtract the cost of drinks, cups, produce, signs, and other supplies from total sales.

How much they make will depend on what they sell, how much they charge, where they set up, and how many people stop by.

Location can make a big difference. A permitted spot with plenty of foot traffic may bring in more customers than a quiet residential street. Either way, I’d have a parent nearby and make sure you follow your local rules.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

What will your child learn?

A small stand teaches your child things they don’t usually learn from doing chores.

They’ll have to set prices, handle money, make change, talk to customers, and figure out which products people actually want to buy.

Watch out MP

Check your city or county’s rules before setting up. Some areas have rules for temporary sales or  food stands, and selling prepared drinks or food may involve additional requirements.

8. Helping Neighbors While They’re on Vacation

When your neighbors go out of town, someone still needs to feed the cat, water the plants, bring in the mail, and make sure everything looks normal while they’re gone.

If your 11-year-old is responsible and organized, this can be a simple way to make some extra money, especially during the summer when more families travel.

How much should you charge?

A week-long vacation can mean several paid visits, rather than just one  job.

Before your neighbor leaves, agree on the price and schedule. I’d also have them write down feeding instructions, plant-watering details, trash-day information, and an emergency contact. That way, your child knows exactly what to do.

This job is all about trust. I’d keep it to families you already know, keep the spare key with the parent, and go along with your child the first few times.

Online jobs are harder to find at 11 because many platforms and payment services have minimum age requirements.

9. Game Coaching & Building

If your 11-year-old is really good at a game like Roblox or Minecraft, they can teach younger players how to get better, explain game mechanics, or create custom builds and designs.

I’d focus on a specific skill rather than simply having your child play games with someone. For example, your child could teach a younger player how to build a certain type of structure, learn a game mechanic, or solve a problem they’re stuck on.

How much can you charge?

$5 to $15 per session is a reasonable starting point.

A session could involve teaching one particular skill, helping with a build, or walking a younger player through a problem.

Can you make money from Roblox?

This is different from making money through Roblox itself.

Jobs

Roblox has a Developer Exchange (DevEx) program that lets eligible creators exchange earned Robux for real money. But there are age and other requirements, and an 11-year-old cannot use DevEx.

So if your child is 11, I’d think of game coaching or building as a simple service. A real person pays your child for their time and skill, rather than your child earning money from Robux.

How to start

Start with people your family knows who have younger kids interested in the same game.

A parent should handle communication and payments, especially when the customer is another child.

If your 11-year-old is good at reading, math, or a language, they can help a younger child practice those skills.

Indoor & Household Jobs for 11-Year-Olds

Not every 11-year-old wants to walk around the neighborhood looking for customers.

11. Mother’s helper (babysitter assistant)

A mother’s helper is a little different from a babysitter.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

Your child isn’t left alone with the kids. Instead, they help keep younger children busy while a parent stays home.

For example, your 11-year-old might play with a toddler while the parent cooks dinner, works from home, takes a shower, or gets some chores done.

It’s a simple way to give the parent an extra set of hands without putting your child in charge.

How much can a mother’s helper make?

A reasonable starting rate is $5 to $10 an hour.

The exact amount depends on the family, number of children, and what your child will be doing.

What can a mother’s helper do?

The work is usually pretty simple.

Jobs

Your child might:

  • Play games or read with younger children
  • Keep a toddler busy while the parent is occupied
  • Help with crafts, puzzles, and other activities
  • Pick up toys and help with basic cleanup

It’s also a good way for your child to get experience caring for younger kids before taking on real babysitting jobs of their own.

How to get started as a mother’s helper

The easiest way to start is to offer the service to people your family already knows, such as neighbors, relatives, or your friends’ parents.

If your child wants to take it more seriously, basic child-care and safety training can help.

The American Red Cross offers two babysitting courses that start at age 11:

Job Listings

  • Babysitting Basics: An online, self-paced course that costs $45.
  • Babysitter’s Training: An in-person course with prices that vary by location. Recent Red Cross listings range from about $135 to $250, including $135 in Orlando, $149 in Fairfield, NJ, and $250 in Fairfax, VA.

Both courses cover basic child care, common problems, and child safety. Having this training can also make parents more comfortable hiring your child.

12. Household Help for Neighbors

Think of this as chores for allowance, except a neighbor pays instead of a parent.

Some neighbors need an extra pair of hands for small household tasks that don’t require special skills.

An 11-year-old might carry groceries inside, dust furniture, organize a closet, tidy a garage, or help with light cleanup.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

How much should an 11-year-old charge?

$10 to $20 per task is a reasonable starting point for simple jobs. For work that takes longer, $10 to $15 an hour can make more sense.

Before starting, have the homeowner explain exactly what they want done. A clear list of tasks prevents misunderstandings and makes it easier to agree on a price.

Keep the  job safe

Stick to light household work. An 11-year-old shouldn’t handle harsh cleaning chemicals, sharp tools, heavy lifting, or anything that requires climbing on a ladder.

A parent should also know where the child is working and who they are working for.

13. Shoveling Snow

After a snowfall, homeowners often need their driveways, sidewalks, and steps cleared before they leave for work or school.

If you’re comfortable working outside in the cold, you can shovel smaller areas for nearby neighbors and make money shoveling snow at several homes.

How much should an 11-year-old charge for snow shoveling?

Professional snow removal can cost $30 to $70 to hand-shovel a driveway.

If you’re 11, $10 to $25 per driveway is a reasonable starting price for a small or average-size driveway.

Snow shoveling depends on the weather, so I’d think of it as a way to make extra money when it snows rather than a regular source of income. If you do a good job, though, you can have customers call you again the next time a storm hits.

Snow shoveling safety

Before you start, make sure you’re dressed for the weather. Wear warm layers, gloves, and boots with good traction. Take regular breaks, especially when the snow is deep or heavy.

I’d also avoid icy areas and steep driveways. If a driveway looks too dangerous to shovel, it’s better to skip the job than risk getting hurt.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

Flipping & Selling Items

Flipping is a little different from the other  jobs on this list.

Instead of getting paid for your time, you make money by finding something at a good price and selling it for more.

Along the way, you can learn how to research prices, spot good deals, and figure out whether a sale will actually leave you with a profit.

14. Flipping Cards, Games, or LEGO

If you know a lot about Pokémon cards, retro video games, or LEGO sets, you may be able to spot deals that other people miss.

This is basically thrift store flipping: you look for underpriced items at garage sales, thrift stores, or local sales and then resell them for more.

Delivery Driver Jobs

How much can an 11-year-old make flipping?

There isn’t a set hourly rate because you’re not really getting paid for your time. Your profit is what you sell the item for minus what you paid and any selling costs.

One good find might make you $5, while another could make you $20 or more.

Start small. If you buy something for $5 and sell it for $10, you’ve made a $5 profit and gotten a chance to learn how the whole process works without risking much money.

Check sold prices first

Don’t assume something is valuable just because it looks old or collectible.

Before you buy it, check recent sold listings for the same or a similar item. Look at the condition, edition, and whether a LEGO set or video game is complete. For LEGO especially, it helps to know where to sell LEGO sets for the most money.

If you want to sell online, have your parent handle the marketplace account, payments, shipping, and communication with buyers.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

15. Making & Selling Crafts

If your child likes making things, that hobby can turn into a little money.

Simple crafts you can sell work best, like friendship bracelets, painted rocks, beaded keychains, or hand-drawn cards.

The easiest place to start is people your family already knows.

Your child can sell to friends and relatives, or set up a small table at a family event, a yard sale, or a school or church fair with your help.

Can an 11-year-old sell on Etsy?

Not on their own. Etsy requires every account owner to be at least 18, and kids under 13 aren’t allowed on the site at all.

A teen aged 13 to 17 can use Etsy, but only under a parent or  legal guardian who actually owns and runs the account.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

The parent is responsible for everything that happens on it, and all the payment details, like the credit card or PayPal, have to belong to the parent, not the child.

So for an 11-year-old, Etsy isn’t an option yet. If you want to sell your child’s crafts online, you’d be doing it as the parent, on your own account, with your child helping make the products.

How much should you charge for crafts?

Price each craft to cover your supplies with a little profit left over.

For example, if the beads and string for one bracelet cost $1, selling it for $3 or $4 leaves a small profit.

Start cheap while your child learns what people actually want to buy. A few dollars per item is normal for simple handmade crafts.

Delivery Driver Jobs

  12. Farm or agricultural help: Help with simple tasks such as gathering produce or feeding animals on a family farm or qualifying small farm. Check state and local rules before starting.

So, what can an 11-year-old actually expect to make?

Here’s a realistic range based on how much work they take on:

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

What drives real earnings?

  • Repeat clients: A single $20 job is fine, but a neighbor who pays $10 a week for dog walking could bring in $520 over a year.
  • Nearby jobs: Five houses on the same street for trash-can duty might take 20 minutes total. Five houses spread across town could take hours.
  • Supply costs: If your child spends $5 on soap for a $10 car wash, they really made $5 after expenses. If they use supplies already at home, they keep the full $10 before any other costs.

Calculate the real hourly rate

One useful way to teach your child about money is to calculate what they actually earn after expenses:

Hourly earnings = (Payment received − Supply costs) ÷ Hours worked

Job Listings

  • Example A: A $10 car wash takes 1 hour and uses $3 worth of supplies. Your child earns $7 per hour.
  • Example B: A $20 yard cleanup takes 45 minutes and has no supply costs. That works out to about $26.67 per hour.

How to reach the first $100

A single $100 payout is rare for an 11-year-old.

A more realistic approach is to stack several smaller jobs:

  • 5 jobs at $20 each = $100
  • 10 jobs at $10 each = $100
  • 2 weekly clients paying $10 each for 5 weeks = $100

How Your Child Actually Gets Paid

Cash is the simplest option for an 11-year-old. You get paid when the job is done, with no payment fees, delays, or account restrictions.

Legal

But some neighbors may want to pay digitally.

Here’s how to handle it.

Digital payments for an 11-year-old

An 11-year-old can’t have their own standard payment account, but here’s how the main apps actually work by age.

PayPal requires users to be 18 or older.

Venmo offers teen accounts for ages 13 to 17 that a parent or guardian must create and manage.

Cash App works a little differently. A parent can sponsor a teen account for kids 13 and up, but the teen is the one who controls the day-to-day activity, not the parent.

Cash App also has a separate parent-managed account for younger kids ages 6 to 12, which gives the child limited features and keeps the parent in control.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

Zelle is a bank-based transfer service. It generally requires the user to be 18 or older and have an eligible bank account, so it isn’t designed for an 11-year-old to use on their own.

Since an 11-year-old can’t independently receive money through these apps, the simplest workaround is to have neighbors pay you:

  1. Neighbor pays you: They send the money to your adult Venmo, Cash App, or Zelle account, with a note such as “For Sam’s car wash.”
  2. You pay your child: Give your child the money in cash or transfer it to their child or teen debit card.

This keeps the payment in the adult’s account while still letting your child get paid for the work.

Where should your child keep the money?

If your child doesn’t want to keep earnings in cash, you have two common options:

Jobs

  • Kids’ debit card: Services such as Greenlight (no min age) and Acorns Early (for kids 6 to 18 ) let parents provide a debit card, set spending controls, and manage money for their child.
  • Savings account: A basic savings account at a bank or credit union can be a simple way to save earnings while teaching your child about deposits, balances, and  saving.
  • Custodial account: For larger amounts your child is saving, a UTMA or UGMA custodial account lets a parent or other adult manage assets for the child until they reach the age set by state law.

Does an 11‑Year‑Old Have to Pay Taxes?

Yes, but only if they earn $400 or more in a year.

The IRS treats any net self-employment income of $400 or more per year  as self‑employment income, even for kids. Once they cross that line, a tax return is required.

Merchant Services & Payment Systems

But most 11‑year‑olds never hit that threshold on paper. Even if they earn money from chores, babysitting, yard work, or small hustles, those  jobs are usually informal and cash‑based, so their reported income stays below the limit.

But if your child actually earns $400+, for example, running a small but successful mini‑business, then you should definitely talk to a tax professional to make sure you file the right forms and stay compliant.

How to Find Work for an 11 Year Olds Near You

Finding work at 11 doesn’t have to mean searching online or approaching strangers.

The easiest place to start is with people your family already knows, preferably close to home.

Delivery Driver Jobs

1. Make a contact list

Sit down with your child and list nearby neighbors, family friends, and relatives.

These are usually the easiest and safest people to approach for a first customer. If your child wants to rake leaves, for example, start with neighbors who have yards that need cleaning.

2. Let a parent handle outreach

Since 11-year-olds should not manage online marketing or contact strangers online, parents should handle digital outreach.

  • Nextdoor or Facebook groups: Post a short, friendly message offering your child’s help. You can use the copy-and-paste script in the next section.
  • Flyers: Have your child make simple flyers listing the service, price, and a parent’s contact information. Give them to neighbors you know.

You don’t need a website or complicated marketing plan to get a neighborhood  job.

Job Listings

3. Keep the Pitch Simple

A short, specific pitch tells the neighbor exactly what your child is offering and what it costs.

Greeting + service + price + question

To make this even easier, here are two scripts you can use. One is for you to post online, and one is for your child to say at the door.

Copy & paste script for Parents (Nextdoor or Facebook):
Copy & paste this script on Nextdoor, Facebook, etc. MP

Hi neighbors! My 11-year-old is looking to earn a little pocket money this weekend. They can help with yard cleanup, taking trash cans to the curb, washing cars, or quick pet visits for a small fee. If you’d like a hand, send me a message and we’ll set up a time. I’ll be nearby for every job.

Script for the Kid (door-to-door, with a parent close by):
Have your kid say something like this:
Currencies & Foreign Exchange
 MP

Hi Mr. Davis, I’m clearing fallen leaves on our block this weekend. I can rake your front yard and bag the leaves for $20. Would you like me to do yours today?

Parent safety note: An 11-year-old shouldn’t knock on unfamiliar doors alone. Walk with your child, or limit door-to-door pitches to people your family already knows.

What this looks like in real life

I’ve seen kids use this approach in my own neighborhood in St. Louis, Missouri.

We have a lot of pin oaks and silver maples on my street. Around November, the leaves cover the yards, sidewalks, and even parts of the street. Cleaning them up is a lot of work.

A few years ago, two preteen boys rang my doorbell. One had a plastic rake and the other had a roll of lawn bags.

The bolder kid said, “We’re going door-to-door raking lawns on the block. We’ll do your whole yard for $20.”

Legal

My lawn was buried in leaves, so I said yes.

They worked for about 30 minutes, taking turns raking and holding the bags open. When they finished, they had cleared the whole yard and left three neat bags by the driveway.

I gave them an extra $10, so they had $30 to split. They divided the money on the spot and moved on to the next house.

It was a simple offer, a reasonable price, and they did exactly what they promised. That’s often all a kid needs to get a first neighborhood customer.

Turn one customer into more

There is a bigger example of this with 12-year-old Reggie Fields, who ran “Mr. Reggie’s Lawn Cutting Service” in Maple Heights, Ohio.

In 2018, a neighbor called the police while Reggie was mowing a lawn.

Jobs

According to CBS news, one of his customers defended him by posting a video about what happened.

The story spread, and his lawn-care business reportedly received hundreds of calls from people interested in hiring him.

Your child doesn’t need to go viral or end up on the news.

The useful lesson is much simpler: a happy customer can help you find your next customer.

Once your child finishes a job and the customer is happy, ask for a referral.

Your child could say:

“If you’re happy with how this looks, would you mind letting your neighbor know I’m taking on one more yard this week?”

A happy customer can be much easier to turn into another customer than a complete stranger.

How-To, DIY & Expert Content

Jobs 11-Year-Olds Should Avoid

Lots of websites list  jobs for kids that are unsafe, illegal, or just unrealistic.

Like who’s going to pay a an 11 year old kid to power wash their deck, lol.

Here’s what an 11‑year‑old should skip, and why:

  • Power tools & lawn mowers: Power washers, chain saws, and mowers are off‑limits. The American Academy of Pediatrics says kids must be 12 to use a push mower and 16 for a riding mower.
  • Heavy home repairs: Painting houses, scrubbing pools, and building furniture require adult‑level skill and carry real injury risks.
  • Major repair jobs: Fixing laptops or bikes is a great hobby, but adults won’t trust an 11‑year‑old with expensive equipment.
  • Coding or web design: Building apps sounds cool, but real freelance clients don’t hire pre‑teens for paid development work.
  • Delivery apps: DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart require a driver’s license and a minimum age of 18.
  • Paid survey sites:  COPPA blocks kids under 13 from most survey platforms. The few that allow minors pay pennies and collect personal data.
  • Working inside strangers’ homes: An 11‑year‑old should never enter a home unless the family is well‑known and a trusted adult is present.
  • YouTube Content Creation: YouTube requires account holders to be at least 13, and Google AdSense monetization requires a manager who is 18 or older. Beyond the  legal limits, building a profitable channel takes years and rarely generates income for kids.
  • Standard corporate jobs: According to U.S. Department of Labor child labor laws, 14 is the absolute youngest age for standard W-2 jobs. 11-year-olds can only work informal neighborhood side hustles or farm jobs.

Some of these sounds great in theory but when you actually stop and think about them, you realize they are just plain stupid ideas for an 11 year olds to earn money with.

Job Listings

Online Safety and Job Scams

Finding legitimate online jobs for 11-year-old kids takes more caution than a neighborhood chore, because online job scams often target people looking to earn from home.

An 11-year-old should not deal with online customers alone. A parent should handle accounts, payments, messages, and any marketplace communication.

  • Never pay to get a  job: Legitimate work should not require a registration fee, starter kit, deposit, or payment for training.
  • Protect personal information: Don’t share your child’s full name, address, school, phone number, passwords, or location with strangers.
  • Watch for fake payments: Never send money back because someone claims they overpaid or paid by mistake.
  • Check age requirements: Don’t use a false birth date to create an account for an online job your child is too young to use.

If your child wants to make money online at 11, the safest approach is usually to sell a simple skill to people your family already knows, with a parent controlling the account and transaction.

Currencies & Foreign Exchange

What Changes at 12, 13, and 14?

Starting at age 11 builds basic work habits, but as kids get older, more types of work and financial tools become available, although the exact rules depend on the job and where you live.

  • At 12 (Physical Independence): While federal rules prohibit minors under 16 from operating power equipment for an employer, a mature 12-year-old doing casual neighbor gigs can start handling larger tools (like walk-behind mowers or power washers) under direct parent supervision.
  • At 13 (The Digital Opening): Due to COPPA privacy laws, 13 is the major digital milestone. At 13, teens can legally manage their own accounts on platforms like YouTube, open parent-sponsored teen debit accounts (Cash App Teen, Greenlight), and take on more jobs for 13-year-olds that pay digitally.
  • At 14 (The Formal Job Market): Age 14 is the federal FLSA threshold for standard W-2 employment. Your teen can apply for formal jobs at grocery stores, amusement parks, or restaurants (subject to state work permits and school-year hour limits).

The casual neighborhood gigs your child starts at 11 act as the training ground for those formal steps at 14, and later the jobs a 16-year-old can take on.

Jobs

FAQs about jobs for 11-year-olds

Can an 11-year-old get a job at a store or restaurant?

Generally, no. Federal law usually prevents employers from hiring children under 14 for most nonagricultural  jobs, so at 11, your child will usually need to stick with casual work and self-employment.

How can an 11-year-old make money fast?

Start with someone your family already knows. Washing cars, walking dogs, pulling weeds, or taking trash cans to the curb can get your child paid the same day.

Can an 11-year-old make money online?

Yes, but the options are limited because most money-making apps and payment services have age requirements. Your child can do things like tutoring or game-related work, with you handling any accounts and payments.

Merchant Services & Payment Systems

Can an 11-year-old legally babysit?

It depends on local rules and the situation, but babysitting alone can be a lot of responsibility for an 11-year-old. A mother’s helper job, with an adult nearby, is a better starting point for most kids this age, with real babysitting jobs for a 13-year-old or older being the next step.

Can 11-year-olds make money recycling cans and bottles?

Yes, where your state or local area has a bottle or can redemption program. Your child can collect recyclables from neighbors and, with your help, take them to a redemption center.

Can an 11-year-old sell items on Etsy or eBay?

Not independently. Your child can make crafts or other items to sell, but you’ll need to handle the account, payments, and other adult responsibilities required by the platform.

What’s a good first job for a shy 11-year-old?

Start with something that doesn’t involve approaching strangers, such as being a mother’s helper, helping a neighbor you know, or making crafts to sell with a parent. Once your child gets comfortable, they can try more social jobs.

How I Researched This

To keep this guide accurate and realistic, I pulled directly from official primary sources, including the U.S. Department of Labor (FLSA child labor rules), the IRS, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and official platform terms for services like PayPal, Cash App, and Etsy.

For earnings, I benchmarks local rate data from platforms like Rover, Care.com, and Angi, then adjusted them downward to reflect what an 11-year-old can realistically charge for basic neighborhood help.

I also factored in real-world observations from neighborhood side hustles (like driveway car washes and seasonal leaf raking) to ensure every  job on this list is safe,  legal, and actually doable for a preteen.

How to Help Your 11 Years Old Make Their First $20 This Week

An 11-year-old can’t get a standard job yet, but they can easily earn real money.

The path is refreshingly old-fashioned: simple, honest work for neighbors who already trust your family.

If you want to turn these ideas into cash in the next few days, keep it small and simple:

  1. Pick one job: Choose an idea from the list above that matches your child’s skills, using tools or supplies you already own.
  2. List five people: Write down five neighbors, family friends, or relatives who might actually need the help.
  3. Set one clear price: Keep the math simple (e.g., “$15 to sweep the driveway and porch” or “$20 for the front yard”).
  4. Make the pitch: Go knock on the door with your child, with you standing nearby, and have them ask in one plain, polite sentence.
  5. Let the work advertise: Do a great job on that first gig, then have your child ask the neighbor to mention them to someone else on the block.

The first “yes” is always the hardest. After that, word of mouth takes over and the work starts finding your child.

Job Listings

A small neighborhood job can teach them how to set a price, talk to customers, finish a job, and get paid for work they did themselves.

So pick one idea from the table, help your child ask for that first yes, and let a good job do the advertising.

You’ll be surprised how fast a kid learns that their effort is worth something. That’s the real payoff behind every one of these  jobs for 11 year olds.
